note: W1-LIBRARY round 3. The corpus was a clerical library: measured against per-skill vocabularies, axes-maces, greatweapons and shieldcraft scored ZERO across all 70 books, and polearms was single-book noise. A province with 87 named weapons and no written culture of arms is a seam showing. This file is the Imperial instructional spine of that culture — a regulation, a serjeant's marginalia answering it, an arms-master's treatise, a snob's letter that teaches the axe by despising it, and a bill-man's dictated reply. Two declared contradictions, both about method rather than about fact: whether a shield line may be opened in standing water, and whether a hooked weapon is fit for a soldier. Nothing adjudicates either.

books.title: Standing Instruction for the Arming, Marching and Fighting of Auxiliary Cohorts in the Province of Black Marsh
books.author: Sixth issue, over the name of Legate Cassia Verano, Provincial Office at Gideon. Supersedes the fifth issue, which remains in force at Blackrose only
books.unreliability: Mostly right, and written by people who have actually buried men. Section 9 is the exception and it is lethal: the locked line is prescribed for standing water on the authority of a battle fought on a dry causeway, and the instruction forbids the one thing that saves the rank. No book in the game corrects it. A serjeant does, in the margin of his own copy, and he is disregarded.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Prescribes the three-rank locked shield line in standing water and forbids opening it, on the authority of an engagement fought on dry stone. The garrison bill section is sound, the axe section is sound, section 9 kills the second rank.

contradicts.on: whether the shield line may be opened in standing water

books.text:
STANDING INSTRUCTION FOR THE ARMING, MARCHING AND FIGHTING OF AUXILIARY COHORTS IN THE PROVINCE OF BLACK MARSH.

Sixth issue. To be held by every serjeant at the rank of file-leader and above. A cohort that has lost its copy is to apply to the Provincial Office at Gideon and is to be charged 8 drakes for the replacement.

1. WHAT THIS BOOK IS FOR.

The Legion has fought in this province for a long time and has written down almost nothing, because the men who learned the most about it did not come home to write. Five issues of this instruction were compiled in Cyrodiil by officers who had not served here. This one was compiled at Gideon by officers who had. Where the two disagree, this one is to be followed.

A recruit sent out from the interior of the Empire arrives believing three things, and all three will kill him. He believes the ground is ground. He believes an enemy he cannot see is not there. He believes that when he is tired he may rest. Break him of the first in his first week, of the second in his first month, and of the third by making him march when he is tired, which is the only method that has ever worked.

2. THE ORDER OF ARMING.

Boots. Belt. Shield. Sword. Everything else afterwards, and if there is no time for everything else, there was never going to be.

A man who arms in that order can be in the line in under a minute from sleep. A man who begins with his cuirass will be found half-dressed and dead beside it. We have found several.

3. THE SHIELD.

The garrison kite is the arm of this cohort and it is the reason the cohort exists. Nothing else the Empire has brought to this province works as well as it does. A recruit who is issued one will complain of the weight for a month and will then refuse to be parted from it.

Learn its edges before you learn its face. The kite covers from the collarbone to below the knee and covers a shoulder's width to either side of the wrist, and a blow that arrives from outside that width does not glance off it. The blow lands as though the shield were on the other man's arm. There is a habit among recruits of raising the shield toward a shout, and the shout is usually made by a man who intends to be shouting from the other side of you when the blow lands.

So: the shield is turned, not lifted. Turn from the hips. A recruit who learns to turn from the elbow will spend the rest of his service tiring in the first minute of every fight and blaming his rations.

4. THE SHIELD, CONTINUED. ON THE BOSS.

The face of the shield stops things. The rim and the boss do work. A shield used only to stop things is half a shield and its owner is half a soldier.

Drill the shove until it is done without thought. The shove is not a blow and it is not intended to hurt. It is intended to put a man's weight where his weight was not, and a man who has been moved half a pace has for a moment no arm to hit you with. That moment is your whole trade. Every serjeant reading this has watched a recruit shove a man beautifully and then stand admiring it.

5. THE SWORD.

The garrison sword is a short, plain, heavy-tipped blade and there is nothing to say about it that a month of drill will not say better. It is issued because it can be used badly by a tired man in a crowd without cutting the man beside him. That is its entire virtue and it is a considerable one.

The auxiliary who has grown up here will bring his own. Let him, within reason. A marsh-guard shortsword carried low and thrown from the hip is a real weapon in real hands and the men who carry them have been carrying them since they could walk. Do not issue a Kothringi bronze to anyone. They are handsome, they are old, and they bend.

6. THE BILL.

Every file is to carry 2 bills and they are to be given to the two largest men in it, not the two cleverest. The garrison bill hooks. Against a mounted man there is nothing better in the Empire's arsenal, and there are no mounted men here, so its use in this province is against boats, against a shield rim, and against the back of a knee.

Bill-men stand in the second rank and reach over the first. Their instruction is short and it is the same at every drill: *low, and pull*. A bill that goes in high has hit a shield and achieved nothing. A bill that goes in low has taken a man's leg out from under him and the first rank finishes what the second rank started.

7. THE AXE.

The Provincial Office issues no axes. Every cohort in this province carries them anyway and the Provincial Office is aware of it.

An officer newly arrived will want to stop this and should not. The auxiliary's shell-splitter is a wood-axe and a boat-axe and a shellfish tool and its owner has done ten thousand honest strokes with it before ever swinging it at a man. He does not need to be taught to use it. He needs to be taught not to swing it where his own file is standing, which is a different lesson and takes a day.

Where the axe earns its place is against a shield. A sword rings off a good shield all afternoon. An axe goes into the rim and stays there, and the man behind it must choose between his shield and his balance. The hatchets the marsh-guards carry near the head do not split a rim so much as hook it and drag it down, and a shield dragged down is a face uncovered.

8. THE GREAT WEAPONS.

No. Not in the line. A man swinging a claymore in a locked rank is a danger to four of his own and the Empire has paid for that lesson twice within living memory.

There is a place for them and it is outside the line: at a gate, in a lane, on a jetty, anywhere a single man must hold a width no two men can hold. Choose him for temperament and not for size. The great weapons punish a man who is frightened into hurrying, because they cannot be recalled once they are begun.

9. THE LINE IN WATER.

The cohort will frequently be required to hold a line in standing water. The instruction is the same as on dry ground and is to be followed as strictly.

Three ranks. Shields locked, rim over rim, the second rank's rim resting on the first rank's shoulder. The line does not open. Whatever comes at it, however it comes, the line does not open, and a file-leader who orders his file to open in water is to be broken to the ranks the same day.

The reasoning is set out in the fourth issue and has not been improved on since. At the Drowned Ford the line held for the better part of an afternoon against a force that was never counted, and it held because it did not open, and every account of that day agrees that the men who died were the men who broke rearward. Water is a discomfort. It is not a reason.

Officers will hear from local men that a rank standing in water above the knee cannot recover a man who has gone down, and that a locked line cannot let him up. This is true and it is not an argument for opening the line. It is an argument for not going down.

10. THE MARCH.

Twelve miles is a day here. An officer who plans on twenty will arrive with a cohort that cannot fight, and there is no fight in this province worth arriving to without a cohort that can fight.

Rest on the hour, in the water if there is nowhere dry, standing. A man who sits down in this country in wet boots does not get up the same man.

11. WHAT TO DO WHEN YOU CANNOT SEE THEM.

You will not usually see them. Accept it early. The auxiliaries you have recruited here can often see them and will not always say so, and an officer who punishes an auxiliary for being right is not going to be told again.

Halt. Face outward. Wait. This province has never once rewarded a cohort for hurrying and has repeatedly rewarded one for standing still and being boring to attack.

12. LAST.

Write down what happened. Write it even where it makes the cohort look poor, and especially where it makes you look poor, because five issues of this instruction were written by men who were guessing, and the guessing is what this issue exists to end.

books.title: What Is Written in the Back of Serjeant Attus Brell's Sixth Issue
books.author: Attus Brell, file-leader and then serjeant, Ninth Cohort, 22 years, most of them wet
books.unreliability: He is right about section 9 and he cannot prove it, and he knows he cannot prove it, and he says so. He is also comprehensively wrong about the bill, which he has disliked since a bill-man dropped one on his foot at Thorn, and he never mentions the foot.

contradicts.on: whether the shield line may be opened in standing water

books.text:
I've kept this book 9 years and I've never written in it and I'm writing in it now because Verano's dead and can't be argued with any other way.

The rest of it is good. I want that down first. Sections 1 through 8 are the best writing the Legion has ever done about this province and I'd put a copy in the hand of every recruit who came off the boat if the Office would pay for it. The bit about arming in order — boots, belt, shield, sword — I've used that on every recruit I ever had and I've never lost one half-dressed. The bit about not punishing an auxiliary for being right, that's worth the whole book.

Section 9 is going to keep killing men and I can't make anybody listen.

Here's what it says. Three ranks, locked, and the line doesn't open, and a file-leader who opens it goes back to the ranks that day. Here's what happens.

Water above the knee. Doesn't need to be deep. Knee-deep and a bit of a run on it. First rank's got the whole weight of the second rank's rim on his shoulder and he's braced forward into it because that's the drill. Something hits the line hard, or the bottom goes soft under one man, or he just tires — and he goes down. Now. He's under. He's a foot under and he's got 60 pounds of kit on and there's a shield rim across the back of his neck holding him there, and it's OUR shield rim, and the man holding it can't lift it without breaking the lock, and breaking the lock is what Verano says gets you broken to the ranks.

I've watched it four times. Twice I opened and got him up and got shouted at. Twice I didn't.

Do you want to know what the difference was? The difference was who was standing behind me.

Now the Ford. Everybody quotes the Ford at me. The line held at the Ford, the line didn't open at the Ford, the men who died at the Ford were the ones who broke rearward.

I wasn't at the Ford. I've talked to 3 men who were, and here's the thing nobody's put in the book: it's a ford. It's a stone causeway. There's a reason people cross the river there. The water was over their boots and not over their knees and the bottom under them was Kothringi cut stone that doesn't go soft. Verano took a rule that was true on a paved crossing and wrote it down for a swamp.

I've said this to 2 officers and both of them told me the same thing, and it wasn't that I was wrong. It was that if the instruction says the line may open at the file-leader's discretion, then every frightened file-leader in the province opens the line, and then you haven't got a line at all, you've got 300 men standing in water on their own. And I know that. I do know that. I've seen a line come apart and it's the worst thing I've ever seen and it takes about 4 seconds.

So I'm not asking for discretion. I'm asking for a WORD. Give me a word to shout that means *the man in the second rank lifts his rim off the first rank's shoulder and nothing else moves*. Not open. Lift. The lock stays, the front stays, the feet stay, the rim comes up 8 inches and the drowning man gets his head out and the whole thing takes as long as it takes to say it.

You could drill it in a morning. I've drilled it in a morning, with my own file, in the wet season, against the instruction, and if any officer wants to charge me for it he can find me at Gideon and I'll show him the drill first.

While I'm in here.

The bill. Section 6 says give the bills to the two largest men in the file. Rubbish. Give them to the two men who don't get excited. A big man with a bill in a crowd is 8 feet of hook going through the space where your own second rank keeps its faces. I've had my helmet taken off my head from behind by one of ours and I've never once been hooked by one of theirs. The bill is a fine thing on a jetty and a menace in a rank, and Verano loved it because he saw it work once at a boat and never had to stand next to one.

The axe section is right. I'd only add: teach them the rim. Everybody who picks up a hatchet wants to hit the man. The man's behind a shield. Hit the shield's edge where it's thin, hook it, drag it down and let the fellow beside you put his sword in the gap you made. Two men and one axe is worth six men and no axe, and I've never got that into the instruction either.

And the great weapons. Section 8 says choose for temperament, not size, and that's the best sentence in the book and I've never seen an officer obey it. They always give the big sword to the big lad. The big lad's 19 and he's frightened and he starts his swing early and then he's got 5 feet of steel going round and he cannot stop it and he cannot get it back, and the fellow he's swinging at has already stepped inside it. Give it to the slow one. Give it to the one who's boring. I gave one to a fenland lad from Blackrose who never said a word in 3 years and he held a lane at Stormhold on his own for as long as it took us to get the boats off, and he did it by not swinging until it was worth swinging.

I'm going to put this book back on the shelf now and I don't expect anybody to read it.

If you're reading it and you're a serjeant: LIFT. Don't open. Lift the rim, get him up, and if they break you for it, they break you for it.

books.title: On the Hanging Guard, and Against the New Grip
books.author: Berethun Cray, arms-master, formerly of the Chorrol schools, now teaching at Gideon to whoever will pay
books.unreliability: He teaches the greatsword very well and he is dead wrong about why the Nord grip is winning. He has decided it is a fashion and a decadence; it is a mechanical advantage he has never tested, because he will not hold a sword that way for long enough to find out.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Argues the high grip on the ricasso is a decadence that trades reach for showmanship. It trades reach for turnover, and the men beating him with it know that and he has not asked them.

contradicts.on: whether the high grip on the ricasso is worth the reach it gives up

books.text:
A word to the young gentleman who has bought a greatsword because he saw one carried through Gideon on a feast day.

You have bought a lever. You have not bought a sword. Until you understand the difference you will be beaten by boys with hatchets, and you will believe you were unlucky, and you will buy a bigger one.

THE FIRST THING.

Everything a greatsword does, it does by going round. It has no small motions. A shortsword has a dozen little corrections in it; a greatsword has none, and every stroke you begin is a promise you have made to the ground and to the man in front of you and you will keep it whether you like the outcome or not.

Therefore the whole art is in the *choosing*, and hardly any of it is in the swinging. A man who swings well and chooses badly is a mill-wheel. I have taught a great many mill-wheels. Some of them are dead now and I am sorry about it and I told them.

THE HANGING GUARD.

Point down and to the left, hands high, hilt at the level of your own ear, the blade lying along the outside of your leading leg like a gate that has been left ajar.

Nine tenths of what I teach is this position and how to leave it.

Why: from the hanging guard every stroke you own is already half made. The weight is up where you want it and gravity is on your side for the whole first half of the arc, and gravity is the only ally a greatsword has that never tires. From the high guard, hands above the head, you are stronger and you are slower and you are advertising. From the low guard you are quick to the legs and you have nothing at all for a man who comes at your head.

How to leave it: you do not lift out of the hanging guard. You *drop*. The hands come down and inward and the point comes up and over and round, and if you have done it correctly the sword has gone from your left ankle to the other man's collarbone without once passing through a position from which you could have been read.

Practise it against a post until the post is ashamed. Then practise it against a post while walking backwards through water, because you are in Black Marsh and nobody in this province has ever had the courtesy to fight you on a floor.

WHAT THE GREATSWORD IS ACTUALLY FOR.

Width. Not strength. Everyone says strength and everyone is repeating what their father said.

A greatsword is for holding a width that two men could not hold, and it does this because the arc is long enough that a man cannot come into your ground without crossing it somewhere. Put a competent greatsword in a doorway, on a jetty, at the head of a stair, and you have shut it. Put the same man in an open field against three and he will be killed from the side by the second one while he is still finishing his promise to the first.

So: doorways, lanes, gangplanks, the top of a ladder, the mouth of a bridge. That is the whole employment. Learn to read a ground for its narrow places the way a poler reads water. If you cannot find a narrow place, make one, and if you cannot make one, put the thing on your back and pick up something else, and do not be proud about it.

AGAINST THE NEW GRIP.

I come now to a thing that has been irritating me for 6 years.

There is a fashion, brought down from the north by way of the Blackwood and taken up with enthusiasm by young men at Gideon who ought to know better, of holding the greatsword with the leading hand *above the guard*, on the flat of the blade itself, where the edge has been left blunt for a span. They call it the high grip. The Nords who brought it call it something I will not write.

Consider what has been given up. You have shortened your own weapon by the length of your forearm. You have thrown away the reach that is the sword's only unanswerable argument. You have put your bare hand out in front of the crossguard, which exists, I remind the reader, to stop things arriving at your hand.

And what has been bought? Speed, they say. It turns over faster, they say.

It looks faster. I grant that. A shorter lever always looks faster, and a young man who has been beaten by something that looked fast will tell you it was fast. But a stroke that arrives at the collarbone in less time from closer in has not travelled faster; it has travelled less far. You may achieve the same by standing nearer, which costs you nothing and does not require you to hold your sword as though you were carrying a plank up a stair.

I have said this in the yard at Gideon and I have said it in print and I have twice been asked to demonstrate. I decline, and I will say plainly why I decline, because the young men have been saying I am afraid. I decline because I am 61, and because a demonstration proves what the two men in it can do and not what the method can do, and because the fen lads who fight this way are 25 and have arms like cables and would beat me holding the sword by the point.

Let them win their bouts. The method is a fashion and fashions go. When they are 40 and their wrists have gone they will hold the sword by the handle like their grandfathers, and they will come to me and I will not say anything, and they will know.

LAST, AND THIS IS FREE.

If you are ever in a lane with a greatsword and a man comes at you fast with something short: do not swing.

Step back once, keep the hanging guard, and let him come to a stop. He has to stop. The lane will not let him past you and he cannot live inside your arc for longer than a breath. He will stop, and he will be close, and he will be thinking about how close he is.

Then drop.

books.title: The Axe in the Hand of a Fool: A Letter to a Nephew Who Has Been Seduced
books.author: Corvus Lentulus Balbo, of the Anvil salle, uncle
books.unreliability: Every fact in it is accurate. Every conclusion drawn from those facts is snobbery. He describes axe-work better than anyone else in the library because he has studied it carefully in order to be rude about it, and a reader who ignores the last line of every paragraph has been taught the weapon by a man who would be horrified.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Holds that the axe is beneath a gentleman and loses to a sword in any honest exchange. His own worked examples show the axe winning, and he attributes each win to the swordsman's error rather than to the weapon.

contradicts.on: whether a hooked weapon is fit for a soldier

books.text:
Nephew,

Your mother writes that you have sold the sword I gave you at your naming and bought an axe, and that you are pleased with yourself, and that you have been telling the household at dinner that the axe is the honest weapon of the province and the sword is a decoration.

I am going to answer this properly, because you are 20 and because a badly answered enthusiasm at 20 becomes a settled opinion at 30, and I would rather spend an evening's paper than have a nephew who thinks like a bargeman.

FIRST, LET ME SAY WHAT IS TRUE, SO YOU CANNOT ACCUSE ME OF NOT KNOWING.

The axe is a real weapon. I have watched it kill men. I have watched it kill men who were better swordsmen than the men holding the axes, and I have thought carefully about why, and here is why.

An axe puts all of its weight in the last hand's breadth of itself. A sword spreads its weight along a yard of steel. Two men of equal strength swing, and the axe arrives with everything it has in one place, and the sword arrives with a fraction of what it has spread along an edge. Against anything hard, the axe wins the exchange. Against a shield in particular it does not glance and it does not ring; it goes in, and it stops, and it stays.

This is the whole matter and everything else about the axe follows from it. Write it in your book if you keep one.

Now: because it goes in and stays, the axe is a weapon of *engagement* and not of *touching*. A swordsman may touch a man and withdraw and the exchange is over. An axeman who lands has bound himself to whatever he has landed in. If he has landed in a shield he now has the shield. If he has landed in a man he now has to get it back.

The good ones — and I concede they exist — have made this their advantage rather than their difficulty. They *intend* to catch the shield. They do not aim at the middle of it, where it is strong and where a hit achieves nothing but a bruise; they aim at the rim, low and near, where the wood is thin and the leather turns the corner. The head goes over the edge and the beard of it bites the back, and now the axeman has a grip on the other man's shield with the whole weight of his shoulders behind it, and he pulls it down and outward.

I want you to notice what has happened, because it is the cleverest thing in the trade and it was not invented by gentlemen.

Nothing has been cut. Nobody is bleeding. And the swordsman's shield is now at his waist and his face is uncovered, and he has one of two choices: keep the shield and be hit in the face, or drop the shield and be a man with no shield in front of a man with an axe. There is no third choice. The axeman has taken away the thing that was making the fight even, and he has done it with a tool he uses for splitting firewood.

The short hatchets they carry in the marsh are worse — I mean better, and I decline to correct the pen. Held near the head, they are quicker than they have any right to be, they hook a rim rather than splitting it, and a man with one in each hand can take a shield down with the left and open you with the right in the time it takes a swordsman to think about his footing.

I have seen this done to a friend of mine at Stormhold by a fenland auxiliary who could not write his own name. My friend was the better fencer by a distance. He is buried at Stormhold.

SO WHY, THEN, IS THE AXE STILL BENEATH YOU?

Because everything I have just described is a *trick*, and a trick works until it is known.

Note that the axeman must land. Note that he must land on a particular part of a particular thing. Note that if he misses the rim and takes the face of the shield he has spent his whole swing to make a noise, and that he is now open for as long as it takes to bring the head back up, which is longer than it takes a swordsman to do anything he likes. The axe has no small motions. It has no recovery. It commits, absolutely, every time, and a man who commits absolutely against a man who does not is a man who will be beaten by patience.

The sword makes no promises. That is its refinement and it is why gentlemen carry it. A swordsman may begin a cut and change his mind halfway and end in a thrust; may touch, withdraw, touch again; may spend an afternoon learning an opponent at no cost. The axeman is buying every question he asks and paying the full price whether the answer is any good or not.

Your fenland auxiliary beat my friend because my friend fought him as though he were a fencer. He was not a fencer. He was a man with one question, and my friend answered it, and my friend was standing in the wrong place when he answered it.

I do not blame the axe for that. I blame my friend, who was careless, and who had been careless at Anvil too, where it cost him nothing.

CONCLUSION, AND THEN I WILL LET YOU ALONE.

Carry your axe. I would rather a nephew who has chosen a weapon and studied it than one who wears a sword because it goes with the coat.

But understand what you have chosen. You have chosen a weapon that will win you every fight against a man who does not know it and lose you every fight against a man who does. You have chosen to be a question and not an argument. And when you are 40, and your shoulder has gone, and you cannot commit the way this weapon requires you to commit 200 times in an afternoon, you will find that the sword is still there and still does not require anything of you that you cannot give.

Your mother says you are happy. I am glad of it. Come at harvest and bring the axe and we will see.

Your uncle,
CORVUS

*P.S. — Do not, whatever else you do, buy a flail. There are men in this province who will tell you a chain is the same idea carried further. It is not carried further. It is carried past the point at which you can get it back.*

books.title: An Answer to the Gentleman From Anvil, Written by One of the Hooking Sort
books.author: Dag Ostrey, bill-man, Ninth Cohort, dictated to the cohort clerk at Thorn because he does not write
books.unreliability: He answers an argument he has heard secondhand in an alehouse and misremembers half of it, and he is right anyway. He also thinks the letter was about him. It was not about him.

contradicts.on: whether a hooked weapon is fit for a soldier

books.text:
A gentleman's letter about the axe has got into the province and men have been reading bits of it out at Thorn for a fortnight and laughing, and one of them read out the bit about the hooking sort being no fit weapon for a soldier, and everyone looked at me.

So. I'm the hooking sort. I've carried a bill 14 years. Write this down as I say it, Neveni, don't tidy it.

The gentleman says a hook is a trick and a trick works till it's known. Right. Everything's a trick till it's known. His sword's a trick. The first man who ever put a point on a stick was doing a trick and everyone he did it to thought it was very unfair.

Here's what I know about the bill, and I'll tell you straight, some of it's against me.

WHAT IT'S GOOD FOR.

It's good for the second rank and it's good for nothing else, and any officer who's put me anywhere but the second rank has been an officer I've had to work around.

You stand behind your mate. Your mate's got the shield and he's got the whole business of being frightened, and you've got 8 feet of ash with a hook and a spike and a bit of an edge, and you're looking over his shoulder at the man opposite, and you're not looking at the man's face. Never look at the face. Look at his front knee.

Then: low, and pull. That's the whole of it. Everything else is decoration. Low, and pull.

You put the hook past his shield — under it, round it, over the top of it if he's a tall one and lazy — and you get it behind the knee or the ankle and you don't chop, you PULL, and you sit down into it with your whole weight like you're hauling a boat in.

He goes down. He always goes down. A man standing in mud can't be pulled and stay standing, there's nothing for his foot to argue with. And a man on his back in a fight is finished, and your mate in the front rank does the finishing, and neither of you has done anything a gentleman would call fencing.

ON WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT ISN'T.

They call it a halberd in the Empire and in the stores at Gideon it's written down as a halberd and it isn't one. A halberd's got an axe head on it and a spike on top and it's made for a man on a horse. There's no horses here. What we carry is a bill: a hedging tool with a hook and a bit of a spike, on a longer pole than a hedger would want, and it was made for cutting brush and it does that better than it does this.

Same family as the spear, and I'll say the honest thing about the spear too. A spear's a better weapon than a bill in every way but one. It's quicker, it's simpler, you can teach it to a farmer in an afternoon, and a wall of spears will stop anything that's ever walked. The marsh-lance the auxiliaries throw down overhand from above the shoulder is a lovely thing and I couldn't do it if I trained till I was 50.

The one way the bill's better: a spear can only push. A bill can pull. That's the whole difference between the two weapons and it's why I've got one and not the other, and if you take nothing else from this take that a hook is a spear that can work in the other direction.

The glaive the marsh-guards carry is a third thing again — all blade, no hook, and it cuts down a lane where a bill sweeps across one. Beautiful weapon. Wrong weapon for standing behind somebody.

WHAT IT'S BAD FOR.

Everything else. And I'll say it before some clever officer says it for me.

It's no good on your own. Nobody's ever won a fight alone with a bill and if you're alone with one, drop it and run and pick up whatever's on the ground. It's got no defence in it. It's slow to bring back. It's 8 feet of nuisance in a doorway. And in a crowd it'll take your own mate's ear off, and I've done that, and I'd rather have been hit myself.

Serjeant Brell says give the bills to the men who don't get excited, not the big ones. Brell's right and Brell's been saying it for years and nobody listens because a bill looks like a big man's tool. It isn't. It's a patient man's tool. You stand there and you do nothing for a long time. You do nothing while your mate's being hit. You do nothing while you're being shouted at. And then his front knee comes forward 6 inches and you take it and you sit down.

ON BEING A COWARD.

That's the real complaint, isn't it. Not that it doesn't work. That it works and it isn't brave.

I've thought about it. I have. You stand behind another man and you hit people who aren't looking at you.

Only — here's the thing nobody who says that has ever done. You stand in the second rank for one afternoon and see how it feels to be the man who can't cover himself. I've got no shield. I've got both hands on a pole. Everything that comes over the top comes to me and I can't do anything about any of it, and I can't step back because there's a third rank behind me, and I can't step forward because there's Brell. I just stand there and hold my mate's life in my hands and hope somebody's holding mine.

If that's cowardice it's a strange sort where you're the one who can't defend himself.

ONE MORE THING AND THEN I'M DONE, NEVENI.

The gentleman's letter says the axe is a question and the sword's an argument. I liked that. I'd only say he's got the bill in the wrong place, because the bill isn't a question OR an argument.

The bill's the ground. The bill takes the ground away from him. He can be as clever as he likes about where his sword's going while he's sitting in the water.

That's what I want said. Now read it back and if you've made me sound clever, take it out.
